source.title: Weird Generalization is Weirdly Brittle
source.authors: Miriam Wanner; Hannah Collison; William Jurayj; Benjamin Van Durme; M. Dredze; W. Walden

page_placements.theme: Narrow training can generalize to broader misalignment

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether fine-tuning on harmful or risky-output data can produce misaligned responses, using different datasets and evaluations from the cited safety fine-tuning work.
record.gate_note: The study reports misalignment outcomes after fine-tuning on insecure code and risky-advice datasets. These bear on harmful fine-tuning, but they are not direct measurements of refusal rates, and the fine-tuning sets contain thousands of examples. Results on benign narrow-domain datasets and context-prefix mitigations are not rows for benign fine-tuning erosion or compliant-opening bypass.
record.test_reason: The study measures emergent misalignment, not harmful-request compliance. Models fine-tuned on insecure code or risky advice are scored for misaligned answers to benign open-ended questions (wish, bored, husband, and so on). No version names this construct. V1 is about complying with harmful requests after harmful fine-tuning, and no refusal or harmful-request compliance rate is reported. The study cites Qi et al. only as background. The findings belong under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude weird generalization, including emergent misalignment, is brittle: it arises robustly only for specific models (GPT-4.1, Llama-3.1-70B) on specific datasets. Training-time context prefixes, even irrelevant ones, largely suppress it, apparently by locking it behind a prompt trigger.
record.recipe_differences: Uses narrow-domain fine-tuning datasets including insecure code and risky advice, with evaluations of broad misalignment and weird generalization; it does not test the few-to-hundreds-example recipe or refusal-rate measure in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Model and fine-tuning dataset materially change the result; the paper reports effects only for certain model-dataset combinations and notes incoherence for some code-fine-tuned models.

fits_no_version.finding: Narrow fine-tuning on insecure code or risky advice yields judge-scored broad misalignment on benign open-ended questions for some models: GPT-4.1 36.6% on Code; Llama-3.1-70B 45.2% on Finance and 40.2% on Sports. For other models it does not: Llama-3.1-70B shows none on Code, and GPT-OSS-120B and Qwen-3-32B show low, incoherent misalignment.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Emergent misalignment: narrow harmful-domain fine-tuning induces broadly misaligned answers to unrelated benign prompts, and the effect is model- and dataset-dependent.

fits_no_version.finding: Training-time context prefixes suppress emergent misalignment, including on Code for GPT-4.1 and on Finance and Sports for Llama-3.1-70B; even some irrelevant prefixes work. The same context at inference re-elicits the behaviour, acting like a backdoor.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training-time context or inoculation prefixes suppress emergent misalignment and gate it behind a trigger.

record.problems: The relevant outcomes are judge-scored broad misalignment, not direct refusal or harmful-request compliance rates. Harmful/risky fine-tuning uses thousands of examples, not a few to a few hundred. Some model-dataset combinations show incoherence; several relevant plotted rates are not stated numerically in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Excluded results on benign narrow-domain datasets, prompt-context mitigation conditions, and non-safety weird-generalization traits because they do not measure the claim versions' specified harmful-request refusal behavior.

untested.parts: No harmful-request compliance or refusal rate is measured after harmful fine-tuning. The fine-tuning sets are 6,000–12,000 examples.
Benign narrow datasets (birds, cities, Harry Potter, medical terms) are scored only for persona generalization, not harmful compliance.
No per-token KL or token-position analysis.
No prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks. Context prefixes act as training-time mitigations or triggers for a persona, not as refusal bypass.
No analysis of why safety alignment is shallow.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V1 labels are dropped. The rows measure misaligned answers to benign prompts, not compliance with harmful requests, so they cannot support or challenge V1. The Figure 3 values for r5 and r6 are recoverable (45.2%, 40.2%). OpenAI's fine-tuning API blocked GPT-4.1 training on Finance and Sports; this is incidental and gives no rate.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not measure refusal rates directly, establish near-total removal of refusal, or test harmful fine-tuning with a few to a few hundred examples.

relation.reason: The introduction and related work discuss fine-tuning undermining safety guardrails, while the study's own experiments address weird generalization.

tranche.reason: The experiments measure emergent misalignment on open-ended questions, a different construct from harmful-request compliance; they do not test or use another listed claim version.

source_check.notes: The cannot_determine states are appropriate for all six rows because their measure does not establish any listed claim version. Context-trigger evidence in §5.5 concerns GPT-4.1 on Birds; some generic irrelevant prefixes fail to mitigate generalization.
